projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harry Shirey was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: [inaudible] '44 Christmas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now you're going to look at me.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Okay. And everything is running. Sounds --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And now, when I -- this -- this documentary will -- with the documentary, you're not going to hear me.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: They're only going to hear you.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So if I say, "Where were you born," you're going to say, "I was born" -- "Where did you go to school?" "I went to school" -- "You remember Pearl Harbor Day?" "Yes. I remember Pearl Har -- I remember Pearl Harbor Day."

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So what we'll start out with is just real -- is real simple, is you're -- you're from Smyrna?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Currently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Were you born there? Were you born --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Born in western Pennsylvania in a little town called Harmony.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So why don't -- here, let's do this. You're going to say -- I'm going to ask you your name. You're going to do your name. You're going to say you're Harry Ray -- Shirey?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Shirey.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Shirey. From Smyrna, Delaware.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Then you say, "I was born in 19" -- bup, bup, bup. And tell me -- and then you just tell me about that, where you were raised, what your parents did, how you grew up, sort of.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And then we'll just go from there. Okay?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Fine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So just go ahead and start. Start with your name.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: My name is Harry Ray Shirey. I was born -- I now live in Smyrna, Delaware. I was born and raised in western Pennsylvania, born in a town called Harmony on September 28, 1922. When I was about 5 years old, we moved to Ellwood -- Ellwood City, Pennsylvania, where my father worked in the steel mill. I graduated from high school at Ellwood City, Lincoln High School. And after graduation from high school, I also got a job at this -- in the steel mill, which was the big steel mill in -- in that area. In 1942, I enlisted in the service in the aviation cadet program. I was not called into duty until -- in February of 1943. I was with the largest group of aviation cadet program that -- aviation cadet men that left Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. There were, I think, three trainloads of individuals. And I went to Nashville, Tennessee. From there, we were sent to -- I was sent to Santa Ana, California. And from there, I went to Tucson, Arizona, Ryan Field outside of Tucson, Arizona, hoping to learn to be a pilot. Due to a number of situations, I didn't quite make it. They told me, "You'd probably make a good pilot, but we don't have that much time to teach you." So it was a -- numerous things happened at that time that -- anyhow. From there, I was sent to Amarillo, Texas for basic training. From there, we were given a choice of what -- one of the jobs that we had -- that the Army Air Corps had to offer. And we were told that we would get one of our first three choices of all the jobs the Army Air Corps had to offer. However, they also said, "You'll get one of your first three choices, provided your first choice is mechanic gunner, your second choice is radio gunner and your third choice is armament gunner." We were then sent to Las Vegas, Nevada, outside of Las Vegas, to gunnery school. And from there, we went to Kearns, Utah. And it was going to be a nice place to spend Thanksgiving and Christmas. However, the day or so before Thanksgiving, we were put on board a train back -- or went back to Salt Lake City and was assigned to crews, to be a crew member of a B-17, B-24 or whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You weren't a -- one of these overnight sergeants, were you? They had a -- they had a pro -- one of the guys was talking about they had that same gunner mechanic or whatever, but that you could become a -- a sergeant --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- immediately upon signing up.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: No. They didn't say much of anything about that. It -- just the fact that we -- we were first told we would -- had one of our first three choices of all the jobs the Army Air Corps has to offer. But then it changed. When the lieutenant left and the sergeant got up, he said, "Yes. You'll have your first -- one of your first three choices, provided" -- and he went on to say the three choices. But no. There were a number of things that took place from Nashville to Santa Ana and so forth that meant a lot. We had testing and all that to be classified as to whether you went to pilot school or bombardier school or engine -- or -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Radio?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Radio or the different -- pilot -- or -- the pilot, copilot, bombardier, navigator, whichever one the case may be. But as I said, I was eliminated from that program and -- but becoming a crew member of a B-17 or on a B-17 crew. It was when we arrived at Tampa, Florida, from Salt Lake City. And assigned to -- as a B-17 crew member. When we finished our training there, we were -- yeah. We were given a leave to go home for a few days, and then came back and went to -- mm-hmm. I'm losing some of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's okay. [inaudible]

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: We went -- we got to the -- Savannah, Georgia, where we were to pick up a brand-new B-17 and start our process of going overseas. The first stop we made then was Fort Dix, New Jersey. Stayed overnight. Then we left there and went to Grenier Field, Manchester, New Hampshire. Stayed there about three days or four days. That was our port of embarkation. And from there, we left and went to Goose Bay. And from there, we flew to Reykjavik or near Reykjavik in Iceland, and eventually then on to Scotland, where we left the plane there, and we were then sent to a personnel replacement depot. And we were assigned to the 96th bomb group, stationed in England, near what is referred to as Snetterton Heath, which is south and a trifle west of Norwich. There, we started our career as crew members. And after the pilots had some training flights and so forth, then we took our -- well, we were on -- we had -- we were on -- had five missions, and everything worked all right, fine. We came back one day with about 20 holes or 30 holes in the plane, but that was antiaircraft fire, not any direct hits. And on one particular mission, I -- after we landed, I was interviewed by the newspaper, and my parents got slips home or people saw it and sent to them and so forth, but -- On our sixth mission, was entirely different situation that we had not encountered anything like that because we were attacked -- well, let's see. There were -- our base put 32 aircraft in the air that day. There was a total of 807 bombers flying that day and 729 escort fighter planes scheduled. And we had been to Berlin the day before, the Berlin area, which completed five missions, and we were due for a 48-hour pass after five missions. But they said, "Well, you go ahead and fly this one today," which was our sixth mission, and it was the 8th of May, 1944. And the CO says, "Don't worry. We'll have you on that train going to London at 5:00 this evening on your 48-hour pass." However, that day, we were shot down by German fighter planes. Our base that put 32 in the air lost 10 planes that day. We were very fortunate in the fact that all our crew members got out without serious injury. The pilot broke his left arm, and the copilot broke his leg when he hit the ground. And I was still in the plane when it exploded. But I also had gunshot wounds in both feet, and I managed to get out, even after the plane exploded. So currently, I say always I'm very fortunate. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When the plane exploded, where were you -- were you waist gunner?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Tail gunner.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were in the tail gun.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Tail gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So they come up behind you; is that how you got it in the feet?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: No. Actually, they came from the front. And in the tail gun position, you're kneeling with your feet out behind you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: You have about this much room on each side your shoulders. And a small bicycle-seat-type seat to -- adjustable about that much to keep the weight off your legs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And your knees are behind you? I mean your --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, my feet are behind me. I'm looking where we had been. The German planes came from the front, through the formation. And as I say, our -- our base that day lost ten planes. Six --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How did you get it in the feet?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, when a gunshot's coming from the front, comes right -- whatever --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: But it didn't hit anybody else but you?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: It didn't hit anybody else to my knowledge. But there again, the tail gun, and the plane coming from this angle is coming --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: -- like that, not straight through.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So the belly gunner was okay or the --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Everyone on the plane got out prior to the explosion. The pilot just barely made it out when it exploded. It twisted him around, and he got his left arm broken above the elbow. The copilot broke his legs or broke his leg when he hit the ground. A couple of the other individuals were wounded, but I don't know to what extent; not enough that they were -- well, I don't know where they were. I mean, they were not -- they weren't severely injured, I don't believe, but the copilot, pilot and myself were all hospitalized that day or that evening and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me more about when they're all jumping out, are you trying to get out of the back? I mean, are you trying to get out of your seat?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: I had stayed at my position almost too long.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You had your chute on?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: I had my chute on. I had a backpack. Most of our crew members used chest packs. You had the harness on, as well as a lot of other stuff on top of it, and the chest pack would have been right in front of the individual or laying nearby. But I had a backpack. And of course -- I don't know if you're familiar with the situation in the air. The aircraft is not heated and it's not pressurized, so once we got above 10,000 feet, we had to put the oxygen mask on. And the free air temperature was 40 to 50 degrees below zero. But we had electrically heated clothes or suits.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: And they kept us alive. And that's how the war was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So now you're plugged in.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: To the oxygen system.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And you're plugged into your suit? Right? Your suit's plugged in?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Right. Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So are you aware that everybody's jumping?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Not completely. I mean, the tail section is -- it's hard to look forward and see what's going on at all, and the intercom system was gone so that you didn't have anybody talking to you over the intercom. And -- but it's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So when it exploded, it exploded over the wing?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: The -- we had two engines were on fire, and the gasoline got to be fine -- yeah. Gasoline got -- the fire got behind the firewall. And basically the two inboard engines was the -- was the cause of the problem. Now, just exactly what blew and all that, I'm not sure about that at all except the fact that the whole front end of the plane was gone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And you were free-fall -- I mean, how did you get --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: The rest of it was coming -- or the whole -- beh -- underneath the horizontal stabilizer, there's an exit for the tail gunner position.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: And I managed and fought to that position until I -- until I could get it to open and get out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So now you're out. What are you seeing on the way down?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, one of the things I saw was a big life raft floating down that had -- when it exploded, it automatically inflated and came out. There wasn't much that I could see except the fact that I was -- when I was getting down quite a ways, I was getting into a group of pine trees, a small forest, you might say, of pine trees. And I know that what they taught us, if you're going to have to use a parachute, was to protect your face and cross your legs in case you were to come down in a tree. I just swung open my arms and my legs and swung right into the top of that tree, and I didn't get hurt at all. But there again, the copilot broke his leg when he went down. But I grabbed a hold of that tree. I mean, the trees were coming up real fast. It seemed like that. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, did you see the -- when you were -- could you see where the plane was going? No?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: It just -- I mean, I couldn't tell you one bit about that. I know that -- that there were pieces scattered around, but just exactly where the actual portion of the plane that I was in, where it landed -- well, I didn't -- I didn't go anyplace to see it or to see anything that I could see anything of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you -- do you remember -- I mean, do you remember being -- you think you were totally conscious when that thing blew up or when you came out?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Oh, I was conscious. Yeah. I just -- get the heck out of here. I mean, that was the -- that was my -- when -- when it exploded, that was -- that was the prime thing. I mean, get the heck out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So now you're down in the tree.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, I unbuckled my chute and slid the rest of the way down. And I walked out of the edge of the -- to the woods or the -- forward of trees and so forth and sit down to use the first aid kit that I had, to -- because I knew the whole front -- front section of my right boot was just -- it -- just gone like that. And I was going to give myself first aid, and the German farmer came over, and he wanted to know right away, "Pistole? Pistole?" And I -- no pistol. "Zigaretten?" I said, "No cigarettes either." In fact, I -- I sort of thought he was offering me one when he held out the cigarettes, and I was -- oh, no. But that was just very -- No. I -- no one mistreated me whatsoever. They loaded the life raft, the inflated life raft, onto the wagon that was there, and after I bandaged up my feet and everything, but -- One of the things that I -- I bandaged up my foot and I -- I thought, okay. Now I got up, had tied things around my foot and everything. And I looked down, and there's a hole in my left boot. And I was kind of disgusted. So I sit down. I took my boot off, took my sock off and in doing so, one of my toes dropped out on the ground.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Ai-yi-yi.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: And I picked it up, and I looked at it. And I thought, "I don't have any use for that." So I bandaged up that foot, too, so -- but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Which toe was it? Little one?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: On my left foot. It was part of two -- one complete and part of the second one, of these -- of these toes on my left foot. My right foot, this much is gone. I mean, it's just -- from here forward, there isn't anything. But -- I was hospitalized and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, talk -- take me through the farmer. What did the farmer do next? He's -- he's now talking to you.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, he just -- when I told him I didn't have any -- have a gun or anything or even cigarettes, why, he and a couple of Frenchmen, they started roaming around someplace and picking up here and there, whatever. And then after I got done bandaging my feet, why, they took me over and helped me to get up on the wagon. And they already had the life raft in there. And so I knew what -- in the wall side of the life raft, I knew there were compartments there. And I thought it's kind of nice to get a drink of water, so I opened it up and got a container of water. And they didn't know whether it was water or not, but I took a big drink of that and of course nice and cold from being at the altitudes we were. But -- And they -- I had a escape kit with me, I mean a small escape kit. And when the farmers weren't watching me, there were two Frenchmen in the wagon with me. I opened up the escape kit. And it had some German money in there. So I gave it to the Frenchman, and he thanked me. And he was also a prisoner, but they were working on the farm. And so what all else happened to that, I don't -- I don't know just what happened to it. I mean, there's a little map done up on a piece of silk-like cloth and thing. But there were some -- a candy bar in there and a couple things like that in the escape kit, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How about -- now, so you were the only one there now with the -- with the -- the German farmer and the two Frenchmen.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Were the other pilots -- I mean the other --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: We were -- we were evidently quite scattered right at that time. I didn't -- I didn't know where anybody else was. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And where were you? Where had you landed?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: South of Bremen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: In Germany?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: In Germany. Mm-hmm. Yeah. We were -- there's an area there that we had crossed nearby, which was Dummer Lake, which was a well-known area for German aircraft, fighter aircraft. And whether they were planes from right there, I have no idea. One report of individuals that I've read their report say there were between 30 and 40 German fighter planes. Another report says there were between 40 and 50 German fighter planes. I have no idea. As I say, you're looking -- you're looking back, not forward. And they came -- well, 10:00 in the morning, they came right out -- you might say out of the sun towards our aircraft. And I could see the going away. I mean, but -- But I -- the wagon took me into this small village or small -- whatever. And there was a big -- a quite sizable big barn. And they took me in there, and it wasn't but a very short period of time until there was -- a considerable amount of onlookers came. But nobody -- nobody was irritated or, you know, anything. And then it wasn't too long until the military personnel came. And he took me. And by that time, there was another individual, which I didn't -- and I still don't know who it was, was there with this German officer, military. And they took us and locked us up in a building. And there was a German work camp, I believe to be, fenced in in the same area, and whether that building that they put me in was part of that, I don't know for sure. And before too long, in the aft -- toward -- towards the afternoon, why, there was enough -- they took us to a -- which was a -- oh, like a small little dispensary- type thing, where they had several beds and so forth. And by late that evening or early evening, there were quite a group, several men from our crew and several from other crews because there were -- there was -- quite a few airplanes went down right then at that time. But it --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Hold on. Hold on. Okay. Let's continue with -- so now it's late in the afternoon, and you're -- you're still in the dispensary?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Yeah. I -- that's the only place I can figure out it must have been, of that -- something of that nature because of the -- I knew there was a prison camp area right -- a fenced-in area right close by, and this appeared to me -- nobody did anything. You know, my feet were already -- I had already bandaged them up, and they didn't do much of anything to that. But they put the pilot, the copilot, myself and three others in an ambulance. And some of the other guys from our crew -- I don't know where they went. I mean, they were in the area right there because I had seen several of them. But I didn't -- I don't know what eventually then -- I know eventually what happened to them, but -- The pilot and copilot and myself and these other three were put in an ambulance, probably 5, 6:00, something like that. And we had quite a journey. And we ended up at a -- at a hospital, which was a German hospital for the work camp area. Or a work camp area. And at that hospital, there were two Yugoslav doctors and the -- there were only six of us Americans. And the rest were Russian, of -- mag -- yeah. Magnolia. Russian, the French and Ger -- I mean, all different nationalities, you may -- Russian -- yeah. I said that three times now. But there was a whole -- just a conglomeration of ones from Poland and Belgium or Yugoslavia and all that type of thing. And there were six of us Americans in the one room, and that's all the Americans were. We were there. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So now they -- they started taking care of you?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: They operated on my foot that night. They trimmed it up, you might say, the best they could. And the pilot had his arm bandaged or set. It was broken right above the elbow. And the copilot had broken his ankle or part of his leg. And -- But that was -- these two Yugoslav doctors were actually prisoners of war also, but they were -- treated us quite well, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, when that was finished, did they ever -- okay. When did they move you into the prison camp, and did they interrogate you and all that stuff?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: I was -- I was hosp -- I was hospitalized at that first hospital for two months. Then I was sent to a German Air Force hospital, which is right up on the Baltic Sea, near the town of Wismar. And when I got there, there was about -- well, the pilot and the copilot and I, we -- they moved us at different intervals, depending on how we were coming as far as our injuries are concerned. And when I first got there, I was put in a room with about -- I'm not sure whether -- I think about six of us Americans. And every -- everything went fine. It was a German -- nice German Air Force hospital and the thing -- we had guards right in the room with us. And I was there -- well, that first hospital I was at was about two months. I was sent to that second hospital, and I ended up being there -- well, I left there about mid -- about the 13th of December, 13th, 14th of December. And sent to the interrogation center. Seven months after I was a POW, I didn't know what the heck was going on. They could have interrogated me all day long and I wouldn't have known a darn thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How were they there?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Uh, solitary confinement. But yet again, they knew -- they knew who I was. They know -- they knew my crew members. They knew them all by name. And they didn't really try to -- Because I didn't know a darn thing, you might say. I mean, while I was in that first hospital was when D-Day came. I mean, because we went down on the 8th of May, and that was before D-Day. And so I didn't -- we just didn't know what was going on throughout the world, period. I mean, most of the -- most of the time. The second hospital there, eventually they moved us up, and there were more of us then, and there were about 20 of us. And we were clear up in the very top floor in -- in the roof area, you might say. But there again, no mistreatment whatsoever. The one doctor used to always come in, and he'd look at my foot, and he'd say, "Weg machen," meaning that I should cut the rest -- have the rest of it cut off, the front of it. I have -- I have the great toe on my right foot. But the great toe on my right foot is not like this anymore. It's like this. Which over the years, it's done. But he may have been right. I don't know. I said, "No. Wait till I get home." Some of the German guards were very communicative- wi -- conversation-wise. We would try to learn and understand them. They were trying to understand us. And some of the nurses -- one of the nurses that was there had a sister living in -- in Ohio. And -- Columbus, Ohio. And -- But we -- we did some things. We bartered with some of the guards. We would -- had some Red Cross parcels. We had the same food that they had to eat. They ate right in the same room with us. We bartered with them a little bit. Some of the Red Cross parcel things were a little difficult -- not difficult to eat, but when you get a whole can of margarine, what are you going to do with it, you know? And he would take it, and next day, he would come back with a whole briefcase full of apples or something like that. And he bartered and so forth. But it was -- it was fine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So once you got to the interrogation area --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, that was five months later. From the time we went down, that was five months later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Uh --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Or seven months, actually.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, once you left there, now, where did they move you?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: From the interrogation center? Well, we went to right nearby, which is Wetzlar, which is another portion of the interrogation center, not the interrogation itself, but a nearby location, where we were sent there to then await to be assigned or where we were to be shipped to. And a group of us that was there then were recent POWs. A lot of those fellows had gotten -- just gotten, you know, just taken prisoners of war a few days before. And when they shipped us out of there, we went to Stalag Luft I, which was predominantly an officers camp, and over 9,000 there. And we were sent there, even though it was predominantly an officers camp, but -- Once we got there, that was -- well, about three days after -- two, three days after Christmas in 1944. And we were assigned to barracks. The prison camp was three -- or four -- four areas, four sections. And we were in the newest portion that had just been built. And there were 24 of us assigned to one room. And we had bunks that were three high. And we had a little stove there that some of the other guys that had been POWs longer than -- or quite a while, they knew how to convert this stove from a heating stove to a cooking stove. And then we cooked a big part of our meals right there in that room. Any Red Cross parcels that we got were usually not whole parcels. They were partial par -- parcels. And we -- everybody combined everything. It wasn't that we we'd say, "Well, this is mine and that's yours." We combined it all. And food. Food, lack of fuel, coldness. Right up on the Baltic Sea in the coldest winter that Europe had had. And it was -- it was okay in a sense, but yet it -- it was pretty brutal. I mean, and the temperature and that -- no -- And I don't mean brutal by personal mistreatment. We didn't have any mistreatment there at all, to my knowledge. And it was -- there were some individuals there then that had been mistreated. I know that. But yet, personally, no. And -- But one of the hardest things to find out later on was that I didn't get any mail from home the first -- for the whole year that I was a prisoner. Not that my parents didn't write to me, but it never caught up with me because the hospital to this hospital to this place to that place and back, you know. And it just never caught up with me, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was there any talk of escape or anything?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Not personally. The barracks that we were in was built up off the ground, not quite waist high, but knee high, I suppose, off the ground; whereas some of the earlier prison camps, the barracks were right on the ground level, where they could and did tunnel, make some tunnels and so forth. And -- But personally, not at our -- not at our prison camp. I mean, not that I know of at our prison camp. Or not where I was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did they actually have guard towers and --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The guard towers. There were over 9,000 of us there. I mean, at that particular --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was there anybody that was -- threatened stuff like the -- you come close to the wire and you get it?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Oh, yeah. There was that -- that little -- only about 2-foot-high wire, maybe not even that high, probably 8 to 10 feet away from the wires themselves, but that wire was the "no." No. From there. You didn't go on the other side. Even if there was a ball rolled over there or something like that. No. You didn't move. You didn't go that far. And -- But it -- it's -- it was basically the same way that -- a double -- a double barbed wire, which would have been probably 8 feet tall, something like that. Oh, probably more than that. Probably 15, maybe 15 feet tall. But the -- the camp -- I mean, when you -- when you watch the program on TV about the -- what took place in some of the prison camps, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: It happened. It -- various things happened, but yet, not -- probably not to my knowledge as well as somebody that was there longer over a period of time, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, when did -- when -- so there was no real scary moments?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: In prison camp?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, there was the -- every now and then we had an air raid, and you didn't know whether they knew where we were or not. And right across the roadway from where the entrance to the prison camp was, there was a flak school for teaching those to -- men the antiaircraft guns. And if that was a target someday, it might have been a real problem, but -- There were -- there were a number of things. They -- they took one of our room -- roommates out, and he was in solitary confinement for about 11 days or something like that. And he told us what took place. And he was in -- he was -- he was held somewhere. I forget where it was. And when they were air raiding -- there was an air raid for the town, and they left him in the one room, locked. And everybody else went to the air raid shelter. And he just kind of broke the door down a little bit and went down to the air raid shelter. And they finally caught up with him and put him in solitary confinement after he got to the prison camp, but -- No. There were -- there were a lot of things that took place that I don't know about probably. And that's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So how were you liberated finally?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, the -- some of the camps in the northern part of Germany and on over into Poland were -- had to be -- they were evacuated. The prison camp where we were at was not evacuated, and the Russians were coming into the area. And we knew that they were getting pretty close 'cause you could hear the cannon fire. And they -- the American commander of the camp literally, you might say, talked the Germans into leaving. They said -- Colonel Zempke was the commanding officer of the prison camp where I was at. He was just one of -- I mean it was, as I say, predominantly an officers camp, so there was quite a lot of rank there, period. And he talked to Germans and said, "Look." In a sense, he said, "You'd better get the heck out of here because you know what's going to happen when the Russians get here." And they -- they did. They left. And the camp was not changed in any manner. The next morning after we -- when we woke up, we looked out, and there's a guard tower with a man standing up there in the guard tower with a white handkerchief around his arm. And it was an American with a GI overcoat on, which we had -- we had some pretty heavy clothing. And then they opened the gates so that you could go between -- not outside the camp, but between the sections of the camp. We could open and go and see if you could find a buddy or something that you might know was there or whatever. And in doing that, I rummaged around, and I found an office. I pulled a -- walked in and I -- nobody was there and so forth. And I pulled a drawer open. And here's all our POW records right in there. And I knew the serial number or the prison numbers of most of the ones on our -- in our hut or in our barracks, and so I just said, "They don't need these anymore." So I took the whole bunch of them, from our -- that I knew the names of the guys. So I have the original of my prison record with the pictures and the fingerprint and so forth. And -- but there again, we were -- we were permitted to go from one section of the camp to the other. And then when the Russians finally got -- they got there in a few days. They were unhappy because the Americans didn't make any celebration of them coming. So finally they said, "Well, let's take the fence down." So we went over, and the fencepost, you shook back and forth, back and forth, until the wire and everything went down. Well, then some of the guys started going here, going there, some of them coming back, some of them never knew whatever happened to them. Because that wasn't -- it was about the -- well, it was the 8th or 9th -- Wait a minute. I'm getting confused. The American -- or the Germans came into the area about the 1st or 2nd of May.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Germans or Russians?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Excuse me. The Russians. And the hostility ceased on the 8th, 9th of May, and the Russians had got there about the 1st or 2nd of May. And some of the guys took off, and I don't know where they went. Some of them come back with this, that and the other thing. A turkey. One guy come back with a turkey. One guy come back with a typewriter. One guy come back with a -- oh, just all kinds of stuff. I stayed right there. I'm not going anyplace. And when the hostilities then ceased, why, I still didn't want to go anyplace. Send the planes from -- send the planes and pick us up and fly us out of here. And that's -- that's what they did. So we flew out and went to France and -- But -- oh, there's -- there's probably a lot of other things that I -- I remember, but I don't, in a sense.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, when you got out and you came back -- where?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: When we came back, we were flown to Camp Lucky Strike or -- flown to Belgium first and then trucked to Camp Lucky Strike, which is near Le Havre in France, an enormously large tent city. And that's where they started really feeding us pretty good. And I mean, you know -- but no. A lot of things took place. The clothing that you had, you had to discard and -- and go through the delousing bit and -- and things like that. But -- and then you were able to send a telegram home. And -- But one of the -- one of the big things that I think about now quite frequently, today's world is so different. Our crew went down on the 8th of May. My parents were notified on the 22nd of May that I was missing. And they didn't know I was alive until August. And that took a big heavy toll on a lot of people at home, back home. But when we left Camp Lucky Strike on a ship, we came into Newport News. And everybody's out on the deck of the ship waiting, waiting, waiting to get off. And we had to wait till the band got there. And they played music while we got off the ship and put onto a train, right on the -- right up to the docks. And we went to Camp Patrick Henry. And it's real close to Norfolk down there someplace. Or at least it was. I don't know whether it still is or not. And two or three days there, a couple days or so, and we went from there to Fort Dix, New Jersey, and had a lot of lectures of what's going on in the world. And we were then temporarily assigned to our home address for 60 days. And by the time that was over, then I went down to Florida for R and R. And by that time -- before that, I was married. I got married. My fiance at that time -- I had called home from Newport News, and my mom -- one of the first things I wanted to ask about was my fiance. And my mom said, "Well, uh, mm, uh, you know." And she stammered a little bit. And I -- "What's going" -- She said, "Well, she enlisted. She's in the service." She was a second lieutenant Army nurse then. Stationed at Camp Atterbury, Indiana. And I was on leave. I mean on leave, pers -- temporarily assigned to my home address. So I got out to Camp Atterbury, and we were married on the 5th of July, 1945. Second lieutenant and I'm a staff sergeant.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's not bad. Is your wife still alive today?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Could have interviewed her also.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, she said, "Oh, I don't know whether they want to know anything that I did or whatever."

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did Allison talk to you about -- about your wife? No?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: I don't -- I don't know. I have talked to her about coming down with me today even, but she said --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, you know what? No. Wait, wait, wait. We're not -- didn't I talk -- did I talk to you last week? Were we supposed to see you Monday?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: No. They called and said to ask me to come about 15 minutes early, so I got here about 20 minutes early, so that's -- no. I had -- she had talked to me and told me about when -- or she talked to me and then said, "I'll tell you -- I'll call you back and tell you what day or what time and so forth," which she did. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, 'cause there's another -- there's another couple up in -- up in Smyrna we're supposed to see next week that were husband and wife. I don't know. I'll find out from her. No. We'd probably love to talk to her.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Well, on that form, it does say something about the, you know -- and I think the original form that I turned in, I did put her name on there or whatever, but I don't recall for sure. But the second time -- I mean, I was -- well, in the Commission of Veterans Affairs mag -- you know, pamphlet that they send out, had the more -- or another pamphlet to fill out if you wanted to. And I asked her, my wife, and she said no. She didn't think so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What did you need?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: I was -- I would like to know what a day in the POW camp looked like, a typical day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me. Or tell -- look this way when you --

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: You mean in the camp that I was at or the camp that was there where I -- well, there's a couple different things, you might say. The -- the first difference that we realized right away was the fact that there's going to be 24 of us live in a room, and we're not going to be served meals or anything or go to a mess hall or anything like that. We were going to have to do it, period, ourselves, mostly. But you got up whenever you wanted to. You could stay in bed all day, if you wanted to, or -- now, of course we had roll call twice a day. And you had to go outside and line up, and the Germans came through, the personnel of the camp, the guards and so forth. They came through, and they counted everybody. And they would go into the barracks and see if somebody was sick or whatever, that he had permission to stay in. And the numbers had to -- had to jive. And sometimes it took a little bit longer, but -- well, the area of the camp that I was in -- one, two, three, four, five, six. I forget how many barracks were there. There was about four or five on this side and four or five on this side and a couple over the other end and a couple down at our -- the end where I was at. So there's -- there's a big amount of people there. I mean, you know. And they -- we had to be counted and count -- but there was -- otherwise -- well, one of the -- I mean, we weren't -- we were left alone, you might say, a big part of the time. I mean, there were -- the camps were run basically on the same way as a military camp at home would be, you might say. You had the commanding officer and his assistant, you know, right on down the line. Colonel Gabreski was the camp commander or the commander of the section that I was in. He was from -- I don't know if you know the name Gabreski. He was a P-47 pilot, from Oil City, Pennsylvania. But there were -- the barracks that I was in, we had almost entirely enlisted men, except there was a room on one end of the barracks and the one room on the other end of the barracks for, like, two officers and where we had 24 men in one room. The -- one of the problems was that -- was cold water, and we didn't have water piped into the barracks. We had to go and get water to bring there. Even the water -- well, the water at the washhouse, you might say, was where you -- you couldn't take a shower, but you had -- you could wash, but you -- it was just cold water. And -- there was -- there wasn't any -- usual -- well, there were in some portions of the camp. There were activities going on; that is, even softball or -- I don't know how they threw, but not in the section that I was in. They didn't have -- I mean, that was in the older section. In -- in that camp there, I have a book at home that reads -- tells you a lot about what took place in the camp. They had some plays that went -- they -- they had -- not plays that came in. Ones that made a -- a presentation, you know, type of -- of whatever you might want to -- I don't know -- I don't know how I wanted to say it, but just as if -- well, like a local place puts on a play. And something of that nature. And there were library books. Not a whole lot. But there were books. Some of them were books on mathematics and different things that some of the men started to have classes and so on and so forth. There were -- I didn't know it at the time, I don't believe, but I didn't get sick or anything, that needed any attention. There were a place there that was a -- a little -- where several beds used as a -- as a -- I'm losing it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Dispensary?

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: Yeah. A dispensary-type thing. And -- but there were musical instruments at a time. They were brought in. Men had formed a little band or something, you know, like that. Not in the area where I was -- not in the camp area that I was at, but in some of the others. And when they moved areas from one area to the other, then they brought some of the -- when they filled up one area, then they would make some of them leave that area and go to the other one to help the other ones -- the new ones get to know what's going on and how to -- you know, how to convert that stove to a cooking stove instead of a heating stove. And they were -- they were helping out like that. But there wasn't -- the only thing that -- at one point in our section of the camp, they set up like a boxing ring. A square, you know. Boxing. And they had a couple of boxing bouts. And in fact, Colonel Zempke was one of those that boxed. I know that. But just in general, we did our own thing. You could go out and walk, if you wanted to and the weather permitting, but these roll calls and so forth. But there was nothing specific that we had to do. And that's --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: All right. We'll do the up and down. And you're going to -- I'm -- Where do you want him to look?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Maybe in the camera.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah. Look at him. I'm going to go out and --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Look at the camera.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah. Look at the camera.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: We're just taking some pictures of you just looking and not doing anything.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: You're not -- you're not going to go away without me showing some of the pictures and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Harry Shirey
sp.p: -- things that I brought with me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Thank you. (Conclusion of interview.)
